title: Catch a model that is 88.7% accurate and misses almost every case
text:
In a published analysis of a national health survey, a model that was 88.7% accurate flagged 805 of 134,897 adults, although about one in nine of them had reported a depressive episode.1 Before you approve a model that looks for something rare, ask for the base rate, the share of real cases it finds and what each kind of mistake costs.
Rare outcomes break the usual defaults, because accuracy rewards a model that never raises an alarm, ROC-AUC flatters one when negatives vastly outnumber positives, and rebalancing the classes keeps the ranking while distorting the probabilities.2 The lab replaces each default with a check you can repeat on your own models.

title: Catch a model that is 88.7% accurate and misses almost every case
text:
In a published analysis of a national health survey, a model that was 88.7% accurate flagged 805 of 134,897 adults, although about one in nine of them had reported a depressive episode.1 Before you approve a model that looks for something rare, ask for the base rate, the share of real cases it finds and what each kind of mistake costs.
Rare outcomes break the usual defaults, because accuracy rewards a model that never raises an alarm, ROC-AUC flatters one when negatives vastly outnumber positives, and rebalancing the classes keeps the ranking while distorting the probabilities.2 The lab replaces each default with a check you can repeat on your own models.

title: Catch a model that is 88.7% accurate and misses almost every case
text:
What you will do
The visual guide and its notebook follow one card issuer through four months of purchases, a scenario written for the book, with 318 frauds among 119,556 transactions.2

Price each error before fitting a model. A false alarm costs $16 of analyst time and customer annoyance, while a missed fraud costs the amount written off plus $25 of handling.2
Measure the model that does nothing. Flagging no transaction at all scores 99.73% accuracy, which is why the lab never reports accuracy again.2
Split the data by time, and catch a warehouse column that lifts PR-AUC from 0.30 to 0.98 although it is filed weeks after each purchase, too late to inform the decision.2
Compare oversampling, class weights and leaving the data alone. All three rank transactions almost identically, and the first two predict a fraud rate about 36 times the one observed.2
Set the threshold from the costs, and then test the review team’s capacity. The cheapest policy flags about five transactions a day for 31% less than flagging nothing, and working every case the team could costs 13 times as much as having no model.2




Total cost over 30 days at each threshold, and the cost of three policies on a log scale. From the visual guide, on data written for the book.2

title: Phase the work so value shows at every milestone
text: Finance will judge an AI control plane program against published payback data, and that data sets a long horizon. In Deloitte’s 2025 survey of 1,854 executives in Europe and the Middle East, most achieved satisfactory ROI on a typical AI use case within two to four years, against the seven to 12 months expected of technology investments.1 A program that phases its work can show value well inside that horizon, one milestone at a time.

title: Phase the work so value shows at every milestone
section: Each milestone has value and evidence
text:
Each milestone has value and evidence
The handbook’s plan runs for 24 months in four phases. Each phase ends in a milestone the business can see, with evidence to report at every steering review.

Value delivered and evidence to report at each milestone of a 24-month plan

Month 8, reusable capabilities

Reuse of published capabilitiesCost per outcome trendRun-rate value of live slices against plan


Month 14, trusted autonomy

All goals metUse cases at full run rate and sustainedNew use cases start on shared controls at lower cost and riskModels swappable without application changesPost-quantum migration on track
The full scorecard at targetCumulative value against each business case



The architecture delivers value of its own before any use case reaches full scale, from spend visibility at month 3 to faster delivery of every new agent at month 8. Each milestone also brings more of a real use case into production, starting with a first slice that works in assist mode and moving to agents that act in systems of record once the controls are in place.
Expectations of AI payback are shortening. In KPMG’s 2025 Global CEO Outlook, 67% of 1,350 CEOs expected returns on AI within one to three years, where a year earlier most expected three to five.2 Google Cloud’s 2026 survey of 2,403 executives found 84% seeing increasing financial returns from AI and 26% seeing returns accelerate year over year.3 Phasing lets a program beat the two-to-four-year benchmark, because read-only and propose-only slices release capacity within months and help fund the controls that the larger gains depend on.
Deloitte’s survey also found that 85% of the leaders it studied use different frameworks or timeframes for generative and agentic AI.1 A program can do the same, judging its early slices over months and the agents that act in systems of record over a longer horizon.

title: Phase the work so value shows at every milestone
text:
What to do next

Agree the four milestones and the evidence for each with finance before the first phase starts, so every steering review reports against them.
Pick a first use-case slice that can run in assist mode by month 3, so the program shows value while the larger controls are still being built.
Set one horizon for read-only and propose-only slices and a longer one for agents that act in systems of record, and report each against its own.

title: pandas groupby, merge and reshape without surprises
text: Most data analysis in Python runs through three pandas operations: grouping, merging and reshaping. The Visual Handbook’s chapter on Python for data analysis teaches all three on an online store’s order log.1 Each one has a default that can change a result without raising an error, and each has an argument that turns the surprise into a check.

title: pandas groupby, merge and reshape without surprises
section: Defaults that change your numbers silently
text:
Defaults that change your numbers silently
The code below shows all three on tables small enough to check by eye. It runs as written on pandas 3.0.
import pandas as pd

# 1. groupby leaves out rows whose key is missing
orders = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "West", None], "revenue": [100, 200, 300]})
orders.groupby("region")["revenue"].sum()                # East 100, West 200, and the 300 is gone
orders.groupby("region", dropna=False)["revenue"].sum()  # keeps a missing-region group of 300

# 2. merge multiplies rows when a key repeats where you expected it once
rates = pd.DataFrame({"region": ["East", "East", "West"], "rate": [0.10, 0.20, 0.30]})
orders.merge(rates, on="region", how="left")             # 4 rows from 3 orders
orders.merge(rates, on="region", how="left", validate="many_to_one")  # raises MergeError

# 3. pivot_table averages duplicate cells unless you choose the function
sales = pd.DataFrame({"store": ["A", "A", "B"], "month": ["Jan"] * 3, "units": [10, 30, 5]})
sales.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="units")                 # A shows 20.0
sales.pivot_table(index="store", columns="month", values="units", aggfunc="sum")  # A shows 40
Grouping drops rows whose key is missing by default, so the group totals stop adding up to the column total.2 Pass dropna=False when a missing key should appear as a group of its own, which it usually should in a report.
A merge returns one row for every matching pair of keys. When a lookup table repeats a key that should be unique, every order that matches it is duplicated, and every total built on the result grows with it. The validate argument states the relationship you expect, such as "many_to_one", and raises an error when the data disagrees, while indicator=True adds a column that shows which rows found a match.3
pivot_table combines cells that share an index and a column with the mean by default, so two orders of 10 and 30 units appear as 20.4 Name the function with aggfunc, or use pivot, which raises an error when it meets duplicates.
None of the three raises a warning, because each behaves exactly as documented. The damage shows up later, as a total that no longer matches the source system or a dashboard that drifts after a supplier adds a duplicate row to a reference file.
The pattern repeats across all three operations. pandas picks a reasonable default, the default hides a problem in the data, and one argument brings the problem into view, at the cost of a few characters. A plain check catches what the arguments miss, because comparing the row count and the column total before and after each step shows at once when a step has added or lost data.

title: pandas groupby, merge and reshape without surprises
text:
What to do next

Analyst. Check that group totals add back to the column total after every groupby, and pass dropna=False whenever missing keys matter.
Developer. Give every merge a validate argument, and use indicator=True while you develop to see which rows failed to match.
Analyst and Developer. Name aggfunc in every pivot_table, and count rows before and after each merge and reshape in your tests.

title: The same survey says 11.29% or 8.44%
text: The National Survey on Drug Use and Health asked 134,897 adults across 2022 to 2024 about depression, among much else.1 Counted as they answered, 11.29% reported a past-year major depressive episode. Weighted to represent the adult population, the figure is 8.44%.1 Both numbers come from the same people, and only the weighted one describes the country.

title: The same survey says 11.29% or 8.44%
section: Why the weights move the number
text:
Why the weights move the number
The survey is a stratified multistage probability sample. Some groups are over-sampled on purpose, so that estimates for them are precise enough to publish, and every respondent carries a weight saying how many people they represent.2 Young adults are among the over-sampled groups, and they report depression at much higher rates, so the unweighted figure overstates the national rate by about a third.2 A weight undoes the over-sampling. Each young adult counts for fewer people in the population than an older respondent does, so the young adults together count for their true share.

Prevalence among adults, computed two ways from the same respondents1


Measure
Unweighted
Weighted to the population




Major depressive episode, past year
11.29%
8.44%


Marijuana, past month
19.32%
16.22%


Alcohol, past month
52.65%
51.80%


Cigarettes, past month
14.34%
14.86%



Depression and marijuana move most, and both are concentrated in younger adults, who are over-represented among respondents.1 Cigarette use moves slightly the other way. The direction and the size of the shift depend on who was over-sampled and on how the measure varies across those groups, which is why no rule of thumb replaces computing both.
Who is in the sample matters as much as how each person counts. The three survey years hold 174,407 respondents, and 34,875 of them are aged 12 to 17, who answer a different set of questions and were never asked the adult depression question.1 They are a restriction on the population, so every figure in the analysis describes adults 18 and over.1

title: The same survey says 11.29% or 8.44%
section: The margin of error moves too
text:
The margin of error moves too
The design changes the precision of an estimate as well as the estimate itself. In the same analysis, standard errors that respect the survey’s strata and replicates were 1.74 to 1.96 times larger than naive ones, so a confidence interval built without the design would be roughly half as wide as it should be.1 With a sample this large, no conclusion reversed, but the reported precision would have been wrong.
A margin of error measures precision and nothing more. It can be small on a sample that describes the wrong population, because it says how much an estimate would vary across repeated samples drawn the same way.3 Weighting fixes who the estimate describes, and the design-based margin says how sure you can be.
Survey numbers often lose this context on the way to a slide. A press release quotes one figure, a vendor deck repeats it, and by the time it supports a decision nobody can say whether it was weighted or how wide its interval was.

title: The same survey says 11.29% or 8.44%
text:
What to do next

Analyst. Use the survey’s weights and design variables, meaning its strata and its clusters or replicates, for every estimate you publish, and report the design-based margin of error with it.
Analyst. When you show an unweighted figure while exploring the data, label it as describing respondents, and keep it out of any headline.
CIO. Before a survey figure goes into a board paper, ask whether it was weighted and how wide its margin of error is.

title: 88.7% accurate and missing almost every case
text: A model built to predict depression from seven survey measures reached 88.7% accuracy on 134,897 adults. At its default setting it flagged 805 of them, although about one in nine had reported a depressive episode, so nearly all of its accuracy came from answering “no”.1 Accuracy alone could not tell that model apart from a useful one.

title: 88.7% accurate and missing almost every case
text:
Accuracy rewards the majority answer
In the analysis sample, 119,664 adults reported no depressive episode and 15,233 did, so a model that always answers “no” is right 88.7% of the time.1 The penalised logistic regression in the analysis matched that score at the default cut-off of 0.50, and its Cohen’s kappa was 0.04, effectively zero.1 Kappa measures agreement beyond what chance alone would produce, which is why it exposed what the accuracy figure hid. A kappa near zero means the model agreed with the truth about as often as chance would, given how rare the outcome is.
The model itself carried real signal. Its AUC of 0.7406 means it ranked a randomly chosen person with depression above a randomly chosen person without it about three times in four.1 The failure was in the decision rule, because the default cut-off of 0.50 sat far above the probabilities the model gives for an outcome this rare. AUC judges the ranking across every possible cut-off, and accuracy judges a single one, which is how the two can disagree so sharply.

Lowering the cut-off to 0.20 finds 39% of the people with depression, at the cost of flagging 15% of everyone for a closer look.1 At that cut-off, 29% of the people flagged have depression, so about seven in ten flags are false alarms.1 That rate suits a quick follow-up question and would be far too high for anything costly or intrusive. Which row is right depends on what happens to a person the model flags, and a cheap follow-up justifies a lower threshold than a costly intervention does.
The outcome is rare enough that people without depression outnumber those with it by 7.86 to 1. Class weighting and resampling, the other standard responses to imbalance, move the model along the same trade-off without adding information, so a team still has to choose where on the curve to sit.1
The Visual Handbook’s chapter on model evaluation shows the same pattern with fraud, where a model that labels every transaction legitimate is 87% accurate and catches no fraud at all.2 Any outcome that is rare enough produces the same illusion, from fraud and equipment failure to an agent’s request that needs a human to review it.

title: 88.7% accurate and missing almost every case
text:
What to do next

CIO. Ask for the base rate with every accuracy figure, and for the share of the cases that matter that the model actually finds.
Analyst. Report recall, precision and kappa beside accuracy for any classifier whose positive class is rare.
Data Scientist. Set the cut-off from the cost of each kind of error, and show the people who will use the model a table like the one above before they choose.

title: About
text:
I’m John Fisher. At Salesforce, I help enterprises architect the data foundation that AI depends on: MuleSoft for integration and APIs, Informatica for data management, and the MCP and A2A protocols that connect agents to tools, data and each other. Before Salesforce, I spent fourteen years at TIBCO leading solution engineering for enterprise accounts. Across both companies, my work has sat where enterprise architecture, integration and data meet business strategy.
I’m also a statistician. I hold a master’s in computer science and mathematics from Drexel University and a master’s in applied statistics and data science from West Chester University of Pennsylvania. At the West Chester Statistical Institute, I lead the statistical analysis for research teams publishing peer-reviewed studies. And I’m building Aethos, an open-source, AI-first programming language for data cleaning, machine learning and AI.

title: About
text:
What AI+ covers
AI+ is the home for my writing. The articles work through what happens when AI agents move past experiments and start acting across real enterprise systems, and through the statistics, data science and Python that decide whether an AI result holds up. Each article makes one argument, gives its sources as numbered endnotes, and points to the handbook, chapter, guide or study it comes from.
The Handbooks shelf and Guides & Labs link to my other sites, where the handbooks, visual guides and notebooks live.
Some of what I write names Salesforce, MuleSoft or Informatica technology. It’s the technology I know most deeply, so it’s often the quickest way to make an idea concrete. I use it as one example of a broader pattern, not as the only answer, and the target architectures I start from are vendor-neutral by design.

title: Adoption is outrunning governance
text: AI agents have reached the largest companies faster than the rules for running them. By Microsoft’s own telemetry, more than 80% of Fortune 500 companies use active AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools.1 Four recent surveys measure how far governance trails that spread. They ask different questions of different people, so each one needs to be read on its own terms.

title: Adoption is outrunning governance
text:
Each survey measures something different
In the table below, the middle column shows how far agents have spread in each study, and the last column shows what has not kept pace with them.

Four studies of AI agents, each read on its own terms







Study
How far agents have spread
What lags behind




Deloitte, State of AI in the Enterprise 2026, a survey of 3,235 business and IT leaders in 24 countries2
Close to three-quarters of companies plan to deploy agentic AI within two years
Only 21% of the companies planning to deploy report a mature model for agent governance


KPMG AI Quarterly Pulse, third quarter of 2026, a survey of 314 US leaders at companies with revenue of $1 billion or more3
62% of organizations are building, deploying or developing AI agents
49% have set boundaries where agents may not make decisions on their own


Microsoft Cyber Pulse, February 2026, from Microsoft’s telemetry and a survey it commissioned of more than 1,700 data security professionals1
More than 80% of Fortune 500 companies use active AI agents built with low-code or no-code tools
29% of employees have turned to unsanctioned AI agents for work tasks


BCG, The Widening AI Value Gap, September 20254
AI agents’ share of the value AI creates is expected to rise from about 17% in 2025 to 29% by 2028
Only 5% of companies are “future-built” for AI, and 60% report hardly any material value



The four results can’t be added up or charted as one trend, because their samples differ in country, company size and date, and each study counts something different. Deloitte counted plans to deploy,2 KPMG counted organizations building or running agents,3 Microsoft measured agents in active use,1 and BCG estimated where the value of AI will come from.4
Read one at a time, the studies still point the same way. In each one, the measure of adoption runs ahead of the measure of control, whether that control is a governance model, a boundary on what agents may decide alone, or a rule against tools nobody approved.
Companies sense the gap in their own operations. In Deloitte’s 2026 technology predictions, 80% of organizations consider their basic automation mature, but only 28% say so once AI agents are included.5 The cost of leaving the gap open shows up in forecasts. Gartner expects more than 40% of agentic AI projects to be canceled by the end of 2027 because of escalating costs, unclear business value or inadequate risk controls.6 Each of those causes is something a control plane exists to manage, which is why the controls need to be in place before the next wave of agents arrives.

title: Adoption is outrunning governance
text:
What to do next

CIO. Ask for a list of every agent in use, including those built with low-code tools, with a named owner for each.
CTO. Route agent actions through one policy enforcement point, so each rule is written once and applied to every agent, whichever vendor built it.
CIO and CTO. Agree autonomy tiers before the next rollout. Each agent’s tier should set what it may do alone and what needs a person’s approval.

title: Adoption is outrunning governance

title: Every AI claim is a statistical claim
text: Every claim made for an AI system is a statistical claim. An accuracy rate, the savings from a pilot and the share of customers who would use a new agent are all estimates from a sample, and every estimate carries error. In my analysis of a national health survey, one model was 88.7% accurate and still found almost none of the people it was built to find,1 which is the kind of number that statistics exists to catch.

title: Every AI claim is a statistical claim
section: What the plus in AI+ stands for
text:
What the plus in AI+ stands for
The site’s name reads as AI, plus the data science, math, statistics and Python behind it. The Visual Handbook’s second chapter sets out how those parts fit: statistics makes sense of data, machine learning learns patterns to predict, and data science combines the two with code and domain knowledge to deliver something useful.2 Statistics asks why a pattern exists, and machine learning asks what comes next.2
Statistics runs through every stage of an AI system, from collecting the right data to measuring whether the system works once it is live.2 A large language model is the clearest case, because it writes by estimating the probability of each possible next word and choosing a likely one.2 When a vendor or a team reports a number about such a system, the number is a statistic, and it can be tested like one.

title: Every AI claim is a statistical claim
section: Questions that test an AI number
text:
Questions that test an AI number
Three questions catch most of the ways a number misleads. The survey analysis shows each failure on real data, drawn from 134,897 adults in three years of the National Survey on Drug Use and Health.1

Three questions to ask of any AI number, with the failure each one caught in a real analysis







Question
What goes wrong without it
What it looked like in the survey analysis




Compared with what?
An accuracy rate can reflect how rare the outcome is more than how good the model is
88.7% of adults reported no depressive episode, so a model that answered “no” to almost everyone scored 88.7% accuracy


Measured on whom?
A sample that over-represents some groups misstates the population
Unweighted, 11.29% reported a past-year depressive episode, and weighted to the population the figure was 8.44%


How sure?
Ignoring how the sample was drawn makes estimates look more precise than they are
Standard errors that respect the survey design were 1.74 to 1.96 times larger, so naive intervals were about half as wide as they should be



The same discipline applies to the model’s own scorecard. A model’s accuracy is a proportion, so it carries a margin of error exactly as a poll does.3 That margin shrinks with the square root of the test set, which means halving it takes four times as many labeled examples.3 A leaderboard number reported without its margin tells you less than it appears to.
None of the three questions needs advanced mathematics. Each needs a habit of asking before a number goes into a decision, and each has a standard answer that a careful analyst can produce.

title: Every AI claim is a statistical claim
text:
What to do next

CIO. Ask for the baseline with every accuracy figure, meaning the score of a model that always gives the most common answer.
CTO. Require a margin of error, and the sample behind it, on any model metric that decides whether a system ships.
Analyst. When a sample over-represents some groups, report the figure weighted to the population and say which figure answers the question being asked.

title: Each OWASP agentic threat maps to a control you can test
text: Security teams judge any agent platform against the threat lists they already use. For agents, the list is the OWASP Top 10 for Agentic Applications, published in December 2025, which names ten risks specific to AI agents.1 Every one of the ten maps to controls a team can put in place and test now.

title: Each OWASP agentic threat maps to a control you can test
section: Every risk on the list has a control
text:
Every risk on the list has a control
The table maps each risk to the controls that address it in an AI control plane.

Ten agentic risks from OWASP, with the controls that address each in the author’s mapping1







Agentic risk
What it looks like
Controls




ASI01 Agent Goal Hijack
Hidden instructions in content, documents or tool results redirect the agent’s goal
Input and tool-result screening at the gatewayAllow-listed tools per agentApprovals bound to the exact action


ASI02 Tool Misuse
A legitimate tool is used in a harmful way
Per-agent tool allow-listsSchema validationRate, spend and exposure limits


ASI03 Identity & Privilege Abuse
Leaked or inherited credentials let an agent act beyond its scope
One identity per agentShort-lived, task-scoped tokensDelegation that narrowsReal-time revocation


ASI04 Agentic Supply Chain Vulnerabilities
Poisoned tools, MCP servers, plugins or models enter at runtime
Only registered, signed and version-pinned MCP servers are callableA private registry of trusted serversAn agent bill of materials2


ASI05 Unexpected Code Execution
Natural-language paths trigger code or commands
Sandboxed executionCode and shell tools only at an explicit tierLimits on outbound connections


ASI06 Memory & Context Poisoning
Poisoned memory or context shapes later decisions
Context only from governed sources (master data, catalog, lineage)Provenance checksSession integrity monitoring


ASI07 Insecure Inter-Agent Communication
Spoofed or altered messages between agents
Signed agent cardsMutual authenticationA2A traffic through the gatewayNo privilege from self-asserted roles


ASI08 Cascading Failures
Errors spread through automated pipelines
Circuit breakersCumulative exposure limits across agents and sessionsPropose-only on stale data


ASI09 Human-Agent Trust Exploitation
Confident, polished output leads people to approve harmful actions
Approvals bound to the exact action and showing the facts behind itApprover drillsLimits that guard against consent fatigue


ASI10 Rogue Agents
Agents act outside their mandate or hide what they do
Registry and scannersHoneytokens and decoy toolsBehavioral monitoringThe kill switch



Several controls appear in more than one row, and they are the place to start. Approvals bound to the exact action defend against goal hijack and against people trusting a confident draft. One identity per agent, with delegation that narrows at each hop, closes off privilege abuse and limits what a spoofed message between agents can do. Exposure limits that add up across agents and sessions contain both tool misuse and cascading failures.
The threat lists keep growing. Microsoft’s AI Red Team added seven agentic failure modes to its taxonomy in June 2026, among them agentic supply chain compromise, inter-agent trust escalation, session context contamination and MCP and plugin abuse.3 MITRE ATLAS has added agent-specific techniques since December 2025, such as AI Agent Tool Credential Harvesting and Publish Poisoned AI Agent Tool.4 Tagging red-team scenarios with these names lets a team’s results map to the vocabulary other teams use.

title: Each OWASP agentic threat maps to a control you can test
text:
What to do next

Developer. Allow-list the tools each agent may call, validate every call against the tool’s schema, and accept only registered, signed and version-pinned MCP servers.
AI Engineer. Bind each approval to the exact action and show the approver the facts behind it, so a polished draft can’t carry a harmful change through.
CISO. Name an owner for what enters the agent registry and another for what approvers are shown, because no gateway closes either risk alone, and tag red-team scenarios with the risk names in the table.

title: Builders need to plan for the 2026 changes to MCP and A2A
text: Agents reach tools through the Model Context Protocol (MCP) and reach other agents through the Agent2Agent protocol (A2A), and both changed substantially in 2026. The pace is already a problem for the people who build on them, and in the 2026 Connectivity Benchmark, 68% of IT leaders said they find it hard to keep up with emerging agent standards and protocols.1

title: Builders need to plan for the 2026 changes to MCP and A2A
text:
Where each change lands
MCP standardizes how agents reach tools and data,2 and A2A standardizes how agents collaborate.3 Both are now projects of the Agentic AI Foundation, hosted by the Linux Foundation.2,3 A third protocol, for agent payments, is moving the same way.

Three agent protocols that changed in 2026







Protocol
What changed in 2026
Where it lands




A2A
Version 1.0, the first stable release, arrived in March 2026 with version negotiation, multi-tenancy and signed agent cards that let one agent verify another’s identity3
Any agent that accepts work from another agent


MCP
The July 2026 revision made the protocol stateless, removing sessions and the initialization handshake, and requires headers that name the method and tool on every HTTP request2
Every MCP server that held session state, and every gateway that reads MCP traffic


AP2
Google contributed its Agent Payments Protocol to the FIDO Alliance in April 2026, where new working groups are developing standards for agent authentication and agent-initiated payments4
Any agent that can start a payment



The MCP revision did more than remove state. It documents how OpenTelemetry trace context travels with each call, tightens authorization checks and deprecates several features with a minimum 12-month window.2 That window is the deadline for any tool that still relies on a deprecated feature. Agent payments are at an earlier stage, and until the new standards are settled, AP2 is best treated as pre-standard.
For MCP, statelessness means every request carries what the server needs, and no server keeps a session between calls. A server can then run behind an ordinary load balancer, since no request depends on an earlier one. For A2A, an agent card is the description an agent publishes of itself, and a signature lets another agent check who published it before it trusts the work on offer.
The cost of each change depends on how agent traffic is wired. Where every agent connects to every tool on its own, each team re-implements each change in its own code and on its own schedule, and the slowest team sets the pace for everyone. A control plane absorbs much of that work in one place. Its registry can check signed agent cards before one agent trusts another, and its gateway can apply policy to MCP’s standard headers and join every call to its trace, so a change to the protocol becomes a change to one policy, and the same traces show which tools still call a deprecated feature as the window closes.

title: Builders need to plan for the 2026 changes to MCP and A2A
text:
What to do next

Developer. List every MCP server you run, and check which ones still hold session state or leave out the method and tool headers, starting with the servers your production agents call most.
AI Engineer. Require a signed agent card before an agent accepts work from another agent, and give no privilege to roles an agent asserts about itself.
Developer and AI Engineer. Track the MCP deprecations against their 12-month window, and keep any payment flow built on AP2 behind a person’s approval while the standards work continues.

title: What an enterprise AI control plane is
text: The hyperscalers now describe their agent platforms as control planes, and Microsoft calls Agent 365 “the control-plane for AI agents.”1 A label that every vendor can claim helps a buyer only when it means something that can be tested. A short definition and three capabilities give it that meaning, and each capability turns into a question to ask before anyone signs a contract.

title: What an enterprise AI control plane is
text:
A definition with edges
A Deloitte Insights analysis from August 2026 defines an enterprise control plane as a governed, intelligent layer that mediates decisions across systems, deciding who can act, what data can be accessed, how workloads execute and how AI agents operate within defined cost, latency and regulatory boundaries.2 It resembles service-oriented architecture, but it is event-driven and does more than expose reusable services, because it coordinates workflows as conditions change.
HCLTech’s April 2026 analysis suggests judging a platform by what it governs as well as by what it does, since control planes compete for authority more than for attention.3 The same analysis observes that an agent without identity constraints is automation without accountability.3

title: What an enterprise AI control plane is
section: Three capabilities turn the definition into questions
text:
Three capabilities turn the definition into questions
Deloitte’s analysis rests the control plane on three capabilities.2 Each decides something different, and each can be put to a vendor as a single question.

The three capabilities of an AI control plane, with the question each one answers







Capability
What it decides
The question to ask




Architecture
Whether enterprise capabilities can be exposed securely and flexibly across channels, agents, clouds, edge and on-premises systems
Can agents safely reach what the business can do?


Orchestration
Which model and agent handle a task, where it runs and under which constraints
Which model and agent should handle this task, and where?


Trust, security and resilience
Identity, authority, integrity and control across every human and machine interaction
Can we prove who acted, on whose authority, and why?



A product that answers one question well can still leave the other two open. A catalog of connectors speaks to architecture, a model router speaks to orchestration, and an audit dashboard speaks to trust, yet none of them alone decides who may act on what, which is why the definition asks for all three in one governed layer.
A good answer to each question is something a vendor can show on your own systems:

Architecture. One real business capability, such as checking an order’s status, exposed as a governed API or tool that an agent reaches with its own identity and its own limits.
Orchestration. One task routed to a model and an agent by rules you can read, covering cost, latency and where the data may go.
Trust. The record of one completed action, naming the agent, the person it acted for, the policy that allowed it and the approval, if one was needed.

Most enterprises span several ecosystems, so the harder task is coordinating control planes across them. That is the case for a vendor-neutral control plane, one that keeps identity, policy and audit in a layer the enterprise owns while models and agents come from many sources.

title: What an enterprise AI control plane is
text:
What to do next

CIO. Put the three questions into your next platform review, and ask each vendor to answer them on one of your own use cases.
CTO. Map today’s stack against the three capabilities, product by product, and mark each question that no product answers yet.
Architect. Check that identity, policy and audit records sit in a layer you would keep if you changed model or agent vendors.

title: Choose the right statistical test in four questions
text:
Results from pilots, A/B tests and model comparisons often reach a decision as a single p-value, and if the wrong test produced it, even a perfect calculation gives a meaningless answer.1 Ask which test was used, and ask for the size of the effect and its confidence interval beside the p-value, because with enough data a trivial effect is significant.2
Four questions about the data almost force the choice of test, and the discipline lies in asking them before running anything.1,2 A classic slip is treating paired measurements as independent, as when two models are scored on the same cross-validation folds, and it can erase a real improvement or manufacture a false one.1

title: Choose the right statistical test in four questions
text:
What you will do
The lab runs on a clinic dataset written for the book, with 200 patients, their blood pressure before and after treatment, their wait times at three clinics and whether they were satisfied.1

Ask the four questions in order. Is the outcome numeric or categorical, how many groups are there, are the groups independent or paired, and do the test’s assumptions hold?1
Read the test off the decision map. Switch to its rank-based twin when the data are skewed or have outliers, and to Fisher’s exact test when a cell’s expected count falls below about 5.1
Route four questions about the clinic through the map. Blood pressure fell by about 9 mmHg within patients (a paired t-test), and the new treatment lowered it more than the standard one did, by 11.6 mmHg against 6.3 (a Welch t-test).1
Report the other two answers with the same care, although neither is significant. Satisfaction shows no clear link to treatment (a p-value of about 0.27), and wait times do not differ by clinic under ANOVA or under its rank-based twin.1
Close each result with its p-value, effect size and confidence interval, as the review chapter does for the five case studies that follow it.2




The decision map from the visual guide. Start from the outcome, follow the number of groups and the design, and read off the test, with its rank-based fallback after the slash.1

title: Quote a survey figure with its weights and margin of error
text:
Strategy papers lean on survey figures about customers, staff and AI adoption, and one national health survey shows how far such a figure can move, from 11.29% of its respondents to 8.44% of adults once its weights are applied.1 Before a survey number supports a decision, ask whether it was weighted and how wide its margin of error is.
Once you know a survey’s design, weighting it and stating an honest margin of error take a few lines of statsmodels.2 The margin needs the most care, because unequal weights make it wider than the textbook formula gives, and it covers sampling error only, so it says nothing about a biased sample or a leading question.2,3

title: Quote a survey figure with its weights and margin of error
text:
Strategy papers lean on survey figures about customers, staff and AI adoption, and one national health survey shows how far such a figure can move, from 11.29% of its respondents to 8.44% of adults once its weights are applied.1 Before a survey number supports a decision, ask whether it was weighted and how wide its margin of error is.
Once you know a survey’s design, weighting it and stating an honest margin of error take a few lines of statsmodels.2 The margin needs the most care, because unequal weights make it wider than the textbook formula gives, and it covers sampling error only, so it says nothing about a biased sample or a leading question.2,3

title: Quote a survey figure with its weights and margin of error
text:
What you will do
A simulated city wants to know whether a parks levy has majority support. Its survey of 1,200 households was written for the book, so the true answer is known and every estimate can be checked against it.2

Lay out the design. The four districts are sampled at different rates, so each household carries a weight equal to its district’s population divided by the number sampled there.2
Plot support by district before averaging anything. Oldtown, the district least in favor, was over-sampled on purpose and supplies a third of the respondents from under a fifth of the city’s households.2
Estimate support twice with DescrStatsW from statsmodels. The raw responses give about 55%, and the weighted estimate is 63%, close to the city’s true 62%.2
Give the weighted figure a margin of error that allows for the weights. Unequal weights cut the effective sample from 932 respondents to about 660, and the margin comes to about 4 points either side.2
Size the next survey. Holding the margin near 3 points takes roughly 1,000 respondents under simple random sampling and about 1,400 with this design.2




Support for the levy in each district, and the number of respondents in each. Oldtown, where support is lowest, has the most respondents because it was over-sampled. From the visual guide, on data written for the book.2
